Using Causal ML to Answer Credit Risk Questions

R
Credit Risk Analytics
Causal ML
Published

June 6, 2026

Most credit risk models are built to answer predictive questions such as: “Who is likely to default?” Causal questions are different. They ask what will happen if we take an action.

Examples in credit risk management include:

  • Will an early-stage collections call reduce 60+ DPD roll rates?
  • Does offering a line increase improve long-term profitability without materially worsening losses?
  • Should a borrower be placed into a hardship program, or would that simply delay an inevitable default?

Causal ML helps answer these questions by estimating treatment effects rather than just predicting outcomes.

Start with the causal question

Before choosing a model, define the business decision in plain language.

For example:

  • Treatment: customer receives a proactive collections call within 7 days of missing a payment.
  • Outcome: customer cures within 30 days, or avoids charge-off within 12 months.
  • Estimand: average treatment effect, or treatment effect for specific borrower segments.

That framing matters because causal ML is only useful when treatment, outcome, and timing are all clearly defined.

Why prediction is not enough

A standard machine learning model can tell you which borrowers look risky. It usually cannot tell you whether an intervention caused a better outcome.

Suppose collectors tend to call the riskiest borrowers first. If those borrowers later default at a high rate, a naive analysis may conclude that calls are ineffective. In reality, the calls may still have reduced losses relative to what would have happened otherwise.

This is the core problem causal ML tries to solve: estimating the counterfactual.

A practical workflow for credit risk teams

The workflow is usually:

  1. Identify the intervention and outcome.
  2. Assemble pre-treatment features that influence both treatment assignment and outcome.
  3. Estimate treatment effects using a causal model.
  4. Validate whether the estimated uplift is stable and decision-useful.
  5. Deploy policy rules around who should receive the intervention.

In credit risk, useful pre-treatment features often include bureau variables, utilization, delinquency history, income proxies, product type, tenure, prior contact history, and macro context available at decision time.

The phrase “pre-treatment” is important. Do not include variables created after the intervention, because that leaks the effect you are trying to measure.

Where causal ML fits

Common causal ML methods include:

  • T-learners and X-learners for flexible treatment effect estimation.
  • Doubly robust methods that combine outcome and propensity models.
  • Causal forests for heterogeneous treatment effects.

For many applied credit risk questions, causal forests are a useful starting point because they can capture non-linear effects and highlight which customer segments benefit most from an action.

Simple example in R

Assume we have historical data at the borrower level:

  • treatment: whether a collections call was made.
  • outcome: whether the account cured within 30 days.
  • X: borrower characteristics known before the call decision.

The goal is to estimate which borrowers are most likely to benefit from the call.

library(grf)

# treatment: 1 if borrower received a collections call
# outcome: 1 if borrower cured within 30 days
# X: pre-treatment borrower features

causal_fit <- causal_forest(
  X = borrower_features,
  Y = cure_30d,
  W = treatment_flag
)

tau_hat <- predict(causal_fit)$predictions

head(tau_hat)

tau_hat is the estimated treatment effect for each borrower. A higher value means the model expects a larger improvement in cure rate if that borrower receives the intervention.

You can then rank customers by expected uplift rather than by raw default risk.

borrower_scored <- data.frame(
  borrower_id = borrower_id,
  uplift = tau_hat
)

borrower_scored <- borrower_scored[order(-borrower_scored$uplift), ]

head(borrower_scored, 10)

This changes the operational question from “Who is risky?” to “Who is most likely to improve because we act?”

Example use cases in credit risk management

Here are a few strong applications:

  • Collections optimization: estimate which delinquent borrowers are most likely to cure if contacted.
  • Credit line management: identify customers whose line increases create incremental spend without disproportionate loss.
  • Hardship strategy: determine which distressed borrowers benefit from restructuring versus standard collections.
  • Pricing and offers: evaluate whether a retention offer or repricing action changes attrition and future profitability.

In each case, the target is not just risk prediction. It is incremental impact.

What to watch out for

Causal ML is powerful, but it does not remove identification risk.

The main issues are:

  • Selection bias: treatment assignment is rarely random in production credit systems.
  • Unobserved confounding: important drivers may be missing from the data.
  • Poor overlap: some customers are almost always treated or almost never treated, making effects hard to estimate.
  • Leakage: post-treatment variables can invalidate the analysis.

If the intervention was assigned using a strict rule or random pilot, the analysis is much stronger. If not, teams should be explicit that they are relying on observational assumptions.

How to make the output usable

For decision-making, treatment effects should usually be translated into business value.

For example, if a collections call costs $3 and the estimated uplift in cure probability is 4%, then expected value can be approximated as:

\[ \text{Expected Value} = \text{Uplift} \times \text{Value of Cure} - \text{Treatment Cost} \]

That makes the model easier to use in operations, because the ranking is tied directly to profit or loss mitigation.

Final takeaway

Causal ML gives credit risk teams a structured way to answer action-oriented questions:

  • Should we intervene?
  • For whom does the intervention work best?
  • Where will we create the most incremental value?

Predictive ML remains useful for estimating risk. Causal ML adds the missing layer needed for treatment design, prioritization, and policy optimization.

If your credit risk team already has intervention history, outcome tracking, and stable pre-decision features, you likely have the raw ingredients needed to start testing causal questions in a disciplined way.
